title: Dependency Injection
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of dependency injection using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates dependency injection.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Dependency Injection** as part of **Software Engineering, Security, and Performance**. Build reproducibility depends on the Gradle Wrapper, compatible plugin/toolchain versions, declared dependency scopes, and repeatable test/build commands. Use the subtopics—Constructor Injection, Interface-Based Dependencies, Manual Versus Framework-Based Injection—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Professional applications need repeatable tests, clear APIs, dependable dependencies, security checks, and observable failures. Apply this concept in small steps before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.text: Start with constructor injection. Then compare it with interface-based dependencies. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Constructor Injection
items.text: Constructor Injection should support a clear object invariant: make valid states easy to represent, restrict mutation to the intended API, and keep initialization and dependencies explicit.

items.title: Interface-Based Dependencies
items.text: Interface-Based Dependencies should support a clear object invariant: make valid states easy to represent, restrict mutation to the intended API, and keep initialization and dependencies explicit.

items.text: Manual Versus Framework-Based Injection is one part of dependency injection. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the project that declares the necessary JVM, coroutine, networking, database, or serialization dependencies. Never commit real secrets.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: The newest version of every plugin and library is always mutually compatible.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.
